lesson_title: One Road or Many: Ohm's Law and Resistor Networks
hook_text: Add a resistor and the total resistance DROPS? It can — if you add it sideways. This trick runs your whole house.
clip_script: Try this riddle: you wire an extra resistor into a circuit, and the total resistance goes DOWN. How is that possible? Think about traffic. Resistors in a line are checkpoints on a single road — every car crawls through all of them, so each new checkpoint slows the whole road. Just add them: 6 plus 12 is 18 ohms. But wire a resistor in PARALLEL and you haven't planted a checkpoint — you've opened a brand-new street between the same two intersections. More streets, more cars moving, LESS overall opposition. That same 6 and 12 side by side? Four ohms. Below either one. Product over sum: 72 over 18. Your home runs on this trick — every appliance on its own street, all of them getting the full 230 volts, each one switching off without touching the rest. Then comes the classic circuit: one resistor feeding a parallel pair. Four moves, always the same: SHRINK the network to one number. Find the TOTAL current. SPEND the volts around the loop. SPLIT the amps at the junction — the smaller resistor grabs the bigger share. And audit yourself like a bookkeeper: the branch currents must add back to what arrived. When the books balance, the answer is safe.
visual_style: Animated cars crawling through checkpoints on one road, then streaming across three parallel streets; circuit diagrams morphing into street maps and back; a four-step checklist stamping over a fully solved network.
mood: Street-smart and assured — the circuit as a town you already know how to drive.
pacing: Riddle hook, flowing traffic middle, brisk four-beat method ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and walk any circuit in four moves.
